blocks.content: If you strip an operating system down to what it actually does all day, it comes down to a handful of core jobs. It manages the processor, the memory, the files, the devices, and the safety of the whole system, all at once and all invisibly.

These functions are the reason the operating system exists. Every one of them is about taking a limited, fussy piece of hardware and turning it into something many programs can share fairly and safely, without ever having to know the messy details.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308715-282757516.png
1. The Big Picture

An operating system is a resource manager. The machine has a fixed amount of processor time, memory, storage, and device access, and many programs want all of it at once. The operating system stands in the middle and shares these resources out.

It also acts as a translator. Programs speak in simple, general requests, and the operating system turns those into the specific actions the hardware needs. These two roles, managing resources and hiding hardware, run through every function that follows.

["The operating system manages limited hardware resources","It shares them fairly among many competing programs","It hides hardware details behind simple requests","These two roles run through every function it performs"]

It shares them fairly among many competing programs

blocks.title: The manager of a shared building
blocks.content: Picture a busy shared office. Many teams want the meeting rooms, the printers, and the supplies. A good manager schedules who gets what and when, so everyone is served and no one fights. The operating system is that manager for the hardware.
2. Process Management

A process is a running program. On a typical machine, dozens or hundreds of processes exist at once, and the operating system is responsible for creating them, running them, and cleaning them up when they finish.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308715-332422160.png

The heart of this job is scheduling. A processor can truly run only a few things at a time, so the operating system switches between processes very rapidly, giving each a small slice of time. This happens so fast that it feels like everything runs at once.
["A process is a running program","The operating system creates, runs, and ends processes","It schedules the processor among many processes","Rapid switching makes many programs feel simultaneous"]
items: A process is a running program
The operating system creates, runs, and ends processes
It schedules the processor among many processes
Rapid switching makes many programs feel simultaneous

blocks.title: Sharing one desk
blocks.content: Imagine one desk and many workers. Each works for a few seconds, then steps aside for the next. Switch fast enough and it looks like everyone is working at once. That is how one processor serves many programs.
3. Memory Management

Every running program needs memory to hold its code and data. The operating system decides how the limited physical memory is divided among all the programs, and it reclaims that memory when a program finishes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308715-847578618.png

Crucially, it gives each program its own private view of memory, so one program cannot see or corrupt another program memory. Behind the scenes the operating system maps these private views onto the real physical memory, keeping everyone separate and safe.

["Every program needs memory for its code and data","The operating system divides physical memory among programs","Each program gets a private view that others cannot touch","Memory is reclaimed when a program finishes"]
items: Every program needs memory for its code and data
The operating system divides physical memory among programs
Each program gets a private view that others cannot touch
Memory is reclaimed when a program finishes

blocks.content: 4. File and Storage Management

Storage devices deal in raw blocks of data, which are awkward to work with directly. The operating system builds the file system on top of them, turning that raw storage into the tidy world of files and folders we all use.

It handles creating, reading, writing, and deleting files, keeps track of where each file physically lives on the disk, and enforces permissions on who can access what. Because of this, you think in terms of documents and folders, never in terms of disk blocks.

["Storage devices work in raw blocks of data","The operating system builds files and folders on top","It tracks where each file physically lives on disk","It enforces permissions on who can read or change files"]
items: Storage devices work in raw blocks of data
The operating system builds files and folders on top
It tracks where each file physically lives on disk
It enforces permissions on who can read or change files

blocks.title: The librarian
blocks.content: A library does not hand you a pile of loose pages, it gives you organised, labelled books you can find by title. The file system is that librarian, turning raw storage into named files you can locate and open easily.
5. Device Management

A computer connects to many devices: keyboards, screens, printers, disks, and network cards, each with its own way of working. Managing all of them would be a nightmare if every program had to know their details.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308715-405547251.png

The operating system solves this with device drivers, small pieces of code that know how to talk to a specific device. Programs make a general request, the operating system routes it to the right driver, and the driver handles the device. Programs never touch hardware directly.

["A computer connects to many different devices","Each device has its own way of working","Device drivers know how to talk to a specific device","Programs make general requests, drivers handle the hardware"]

Programs make general requests, drivers handle the hardware

blocks.content: 6. Security and Protection

Because many programs and users share one machine, the operating system must keep them from harming each other or the system itself. This is its protection job, and it runs constantly in the background.

It enforces the boundary between programs so one cannot read or corrupt another memory, checks permissions before allowing sensitive actions, and manages user accounts and logins. Without this, a single buggy or malicious program could bring down everything.

["Many programs and users share one machine","The operating system keeps them from harming each other","It enforces memory boundaries and checks permissions","It manages user accounts and controls access"]

The operating system keeps them from harming each other
It enforces memory boundaries and checks permissions
It manages user accounts and controls access

blocks.title: The security guard
blocks.content: The operating system is like a guard who checks everyone entry pass. Programs can only do what they are allowed to, and anything out of bounds is blocked before it can cause harm.
7. User Interface

The operating system also provides the way you interact with the machine. Historically this was the command line, where you type instructions and read text back, and that interface is still powerful and widely used today.

Modern systems add a graphical interface with windows, icons, and a pointer, which is what most people use daily. Either way, the interface is the operating system giving you a human friendly door into all the functions happening underneath.

["The operating system provides how you interact with the machine","The command line lets you type text instructions","The graphical interface uses windows, icons, and a pointer","Both are doors into the functions running underneath"]

blocks.content: 8. How the Functions Work Together
These functions are not separate silos, they cooperate constantly. A single everyday action usually calls on several of them at the same time.

Think about opening a photo. Process management runs the photo app, file management finds and reads the image from disk, memory management gives the app space to hold it, device management drives the screen to display it, and protection checks you are allowed to open the file. All of that, for one click.

9. Why These Functions Matter

Together these functions turn a bare machine into something usable. Without process management the machine could run only one thing at a time, without memory management programs would trample each other, and without protection a single bug could crash the whole system.

They are also why software is portable and pleasant to write. Because the operating system handles all of this, a programmer can focus on their actual app and trust the system to manage the processor, the memory, the files, and the devices underneath.
